Lecture 4 Classical Probability, the Complement and Addition Rules, and the Multiplication Rule for Counting

From the axioms to working rules: why equally likely outcomes each have probability 1/n, the complement rule, the addition rule for two and three events with Venn diagrams, and the start of counting with the multiplication rule.

1. Classical (a priori)

  • Idea: finite outcomes, all equally likely. Just count.

2. Relative frequency (empirical)

  • Idea: repeat the experiment many times and see what fraction of trials happens in.
  • Formula:

As the number of trials grows, this approaches the true (law of large numbers).

  • Example: a loaded die lands on 6 in 300 of 1000 rolls, so .
  • Limitation: needs a repeatable experiment, and it only gives an estimate.

3. Subjective (personal)

  • Idea: a degree of belief based on judgment or experience.
  • Example: “70% chance the Canucks win tonight” or “80% chance I pass the midterm.”
  • Limitation: different people give different answers, and the experiment can’t be repeated.

3The Complement Rule

The Complement Rule

The Complement Rule: For any set or event in a sample space,

Example Last example

is the event you get at least 2 heads.

is the event you get 3 heads.

✎ Explanation (added)

The derivation: and do not overlap, so axiom 3 gives ; together they make up all of , so that sum is 1.

A slip on the board: the first line of the example is written “at least 2 heads”, but the event being redone is the practice question, “at most 2 heads”. Only “at most 2 heads” has the complement “3 heads” and the answer . (“At least 2 heads” would be with probability , and its complement would be “at most 1 head”.) Trust the calculation, and read the first line as “at most”.

When to use the rule: whenever the event you want has many outcomes but its opposite has few. The words “at least one” and “at most” are the usual signal.

“At least one of the two” is the union: Bob, or John, or both. Without the subtraction you would get 0.6 + 0.4 = 1.0, which would say someone is certain to hit. The 0.1 chance that both hit was inside Bob’s 0.6 and also inside John’s 0.4.

Working with diagrams like this is easy.

To find the probability of ending up in a collection of regions, just add the probabilities associated with regions in the collection.

Example

What is the probability that exactly one of Bob and John makes their shot?

✎ Explanation (added)

Always fill a Venn diagram from the inside out: the overlap first, then each “only” region by subtracting the overlap from the circle’s total, then the outside last as 1 minus everything inside. Once every region has its own number, any question is just “which regions?” followed by addition, because the regions are disjoint. “Exactly one” is , the two crescents.

Each number shows how many times that region has been counted so far. The goal is to get every region to exactly 1.

Why the center needs special attention

The center lies inside all three circles and all three pairwise overlaps. Tracking its count:

Final formula

✎ Explanation (added)

Follow one region at a time. A region in exactly two circles is counted twice by the first line and then removed once by its pair’s subtraction, leaving 1. The centre is counted three times, removed three times (once for each pair, since it lies in all three pairwise overlaps), and has to be added back once. The pattern is: add singles, subtract pairs, add the triple.

Textbook · Devore — addition rule for three events: Proposition in §2.2, p. 63, with Figure 2.6.

7Some basic counting rules: the multiplication rule

Some Basic Counting rules

Rule The Multiplication Rule

Suppose there are ways to perform activity , and no matter how you performed , there will always be ways to perform activity .

Then the number of ways to perform followed by is .

This extends to sequences of any number of activities as long as at any stage in the process, you always have the same number of ways to perform the next activity.

✎ Explanation (added)

Counting matters because of the classical formula : both the top and the bottom are counts, and listing outcomes stops being practical very quickly. The condition to check before multiplying is the phrase “no matter how you performed ”: the number of choices at the second step must not depend on what was chosen first (the choices themselves may change).

Textbook · Devore — the product rule for ordered pairs: Proposition in §2.3, p. 67; for k-tuples, pp. 68–69.

Example Soup and sandwich

You go to a soup and sandwich shop.

They have 3 different types of soup and 4 different types of sandwiches.

How many different soup and sandwich orders are there?

To count this, our goal is to come up with a sequence of activities that can be used to generate every possible soup and sandwich order. (preferably exactly once for each order so we don’t have to subtract).

To choose a soup and sandwich, we will first choose the soup (3 ways).

No matter how we chose the soup, we will always have 4 ways to choose the sandwich.

Different choices lead to different orders and every order can be generated.

There is a one to one correspond[ence] between possible orders and the number of ways to run through this process which is .

Typed note included in the PDF

(The pasted note shows the same tree drawn left to right with columns “Choose soup”, “Choose sandwich” and “Order”, listing the orders 1. S1,W1 through 12. S3,W4.)

His main idea: build a sequence of activities that generates every order.

  1. Activity 1: choose a soup, which gives 3 branches.
  2. Activity 2: choose a sandwich, which gives 4 branches from each soup.

Every path from Start to a leaf is one order.

Why “exactly once” matters

Each order appears on exactly one path. For example, (S2, W3) can only be reached through S2 then W3. Because nothing is double-counted, you don’t have to subtract anything, and the count is simply

Example Practice

If they have 10 different drinks, how many soup, sandwich, and drink orders are there?

Try it first, then open (worked answer, added)

Add a third activity: choose the drink (10 ways, no matter which soup and sandwich were chosen). The multiplication rule gives orders. In tree terms, each of the 12 leaves grows 10 more branches.

Try it — grow the tree

Change how many soups, sandwiches and drinks there are. Every leaf at the bottom is one complete order, and the number of leaves is the product.

Interactive widget: open the page on a screen to use it.
✎ Explanation (added)

A tree diagram is the multiplication rule drawn out. The number of leaves is (branches at level 1) × (branches at level 2) × … as long as every node on a level has the same number of branches. “One to one correspondence” is the guarantee that counting paths is the same as counting orders: no order is produced twice and none is missed.

Textbook · Devore — tree diagrams for counting: §2.3, pp. 67–68, Example 2.18 and Figure 2.7.

What a typical exam question looks like
  • List a sample space of equally likely outcomes (coins, dice) and find the probability of an event by counting, such as “exactly 2 heads” or “at most 2 heads”.
  • An “at least” or “at most” question that is far quicker with the complement rule.
  • Given , and : find , fill in a Venn diagram, and find the probability that exactly one, or neither, occurs.
  • A three-event word problem like the traveller: set up the three-event addition rule, solve for an unknown overlap, fill in the diagram and read off a region such as “only ”.
  • Derive , the complement rule, or the two-event addition rule from the axioms.
  • A menu-style question: count the outcomes with the multiplication rule and draw the tree diagram.
